title: The Mondrian hung upside down
hook: A Mondrian has probably hung upside down for over 75 years, and it will stay that way.
peek: Piet Mondrian's New York City I, made of coloured tape, was probably shown upside down from its first exhibition in 1945. A curator spotted the clue in 2022. The museum decided to leave it, because turning it could damage it.
lede: In 2022 the curator Susanne Meyer-Büser, preparing a show in Düsseldorf, realised that Piet Mondrian's New York City I had probably been hanging upside down since it was first exhibited in 1945. The work is a grid of coloured paper tape. Its lines bunch together at one edge, and that edge was likely meant to be the top.

bullets.text: The key clue was a photograph of Mondrian's New York studio, taken shortly after his death in 1944. It shows the work on an easel with the crowded lines at the top, the opposite of how museums had shown it.
The dense band reads like a city skyline, which fits the title. A related oil painting by Mondrian, New York City, also has its lines thickest at the top.

The work was first shown at the Museum of Modern Art in New York in 1945, the wrong way up as far as anyone can tell. It has belonged to the Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen in Düsseldorf since 1980 and hung the same way there.
The tape is old and the glue is fragile. Turning the work around could make strips sag or come loose, so the museum decided to leave it as it is, with a label explaining the story.
